idiom_name: Express middleware chain over a CASL ability (AbilityBuilder can/cannot)
implementation_notes: Enforcement is a middleware in the request chain: an application- or router-level function obtains the decision, answers res.sendStatus(403) (or 401) and returns without calling next() when access is denied. Use that form for URL-level rules; for object-level CASL conditions, place a resource loader before the authorization middleware on the route so ability.can(action, req.resource) evaluates the actual server-loaded object. The decision belongs to a single ability object built per principal rather than to route code: CASL assembles permissions with AbilityBuilder().can(...)/.cannot(...) - including attribute and relationship conditions - and answers with ability.can(action, subject). Exposing the ability to the client for UI filtering is fine, but only server-side middleware decides.
pitfalls: Mounting an object-level guard before loadArticle -> req.resource is absent and the check either denies valid users or falls back to a coarse rule -> load the server-side resource first and authorize the instance before the handler.
A guard that logs the denial but still calls next() (or lets an async rejection fall through) -> a deny becomes an allow -> return the 401/403 response immediately.

Building the ability from client-supplied data (or trusting roles inside an unvalidated token) -> the caller can widen its permissions -> rebuild it server-side from the validated session and authoritative attributes.
